questions.q: What must every SOQL SELECT statement specify that plain SQL does not require?
options: A single object in the FROM clause — SOQL always queries one object (plus its related objects) rather than arbitrary tables
A WHERE clause, which is mandatory in every SOQL query
An ORDER BY clause on every query
A LIMIT clause capped at 10 rows
questions.explain: SOQL is object-aware: the FROM clause names one Salesforce object, and you reach related data through relationship traversal rather than joining arbitrary unrelated tables the way SQL does.

questions.q: In SOQL, what does LIMIT 10 do when added to the end of a query?
options: Deletes all but 10 records from the object
Restricts the result set to at most 10 records
Limits the query to run for only 10 seconds
Limits the query to only 10 fields in the SELECT list
questions.explain: LIMIT caps the number of rows returned, just like in SQL — useful for previewing results or controlling governor limit consumption on large objects.

questions.q: Which of these is true about SOQL compared to standard SQL?
options: SOQL supports SELECT * to return every field
SOQL queries run against an on-premises server the developer controls directly
SOQL has no SELECT * — every field you want back must be listed explicitly, and there is no arbitrary JOIN keyword
SOQL and SQL are functionally identical with no syntax differences at all
questions.explain: SOQL requires explicitly naming every field to retrieve, and instead of a generic JOIN keyword it uses relationship syntax (dot notation and subqueries) tied to the org's actual object relationships.

questions.q: Which SOQL aggregate function would you use to find the total dollar value of all Opportunities in a query?
options: COUNT()
AVG()
MIN()
SUM()
questions.explain: SUM() adds up the numeric values of a field across the grouped or filtered rows — for example, SUM(Amount) across Opportunities gives total pipeline value.

questions.q: In a SOQL query using GROUP BY, why would you use HAVING instead of WHERE to filter on an aggregate result like COUNT(Id)?
options: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping happens, so it can't reference an aggregated value; HAVING filters after aggregation
HAVING and WHERE are exact synonyms in SOQL
WHERE can only be used with DATE fields
HAVING is only valid when no GROUP BY clause is present
questions.explain: Just like in SQL, WHERE operates on individual records before GROUP BY runs, so it has no access to the aggregated totals — HAVING is evaluated after grouping, when COUNT(), SUM(), etc. actually exist.

questions.q: What does a parent-to-child SOQL query look like, for example pulling each Account along with its related Contacts?
options: A query that starts with SELECT * FROM Contacts JOIN Account
A subquery in parentheses inside the SELECT list, using the child relationship name, e.g. SELECT Name, (SELECT LastName FROM Contacts) FROM Account
A query using the UNION keyword to combine Account and Contact rows
It cannot be done in a single SOQL query at all
questions.explain: SOQL nests a child subquery inside the parent query's SELECT list using the child relationship name (like Contacts), returning each parent record with a list of its related child records embedded.

questions.q: How would you reference a Contact's parent Account name in a child-to-parent SOQL query?
options: Using WHERE Account = Contact
Using a UNION between Contact and Account
Using dot notation through the relationship field, e.g. SELECT Account.Name FROM Contact
It requires a separate query — child-to-parent traversal isn't supported
questions.explain: Child-to-parent relationships in SOQL are traversed with dot notation on the relationship field (Account.Name), walking up to the parent object directly in the SELECT list.

questions.q: What does a semi-join subquery like `WHERE AccountId IN (SELECT AccountId FROM Opportunity WHERE StageName = 'Closed Won')` accomplish?
options: It deletes all Accounts without a closed-won Opportunity
It joins every Account to every Opportunity regardless of match
It is invalid syntax in SOQL
It filters the outer query to only Accounts that have at least one matching Closed Won Opportunity, based on a subquery's results
questions.explain: A semi-join uses IN with an inner query to filter the outer object's rows to those whose Id appears in the inner query's result set — a common pattern for finding records that do have a related match.

questions.q: What is SOSL primarily designed to do that SOQL is not well-suited for?
options: Perform a full-text search for a term across multiple objects and fields at once
Aggregate numeric fields with SUM and AVG
Delete records in bulk
Enforce field-level security
questions.explain: SOSL's FIND syntax searches text-based fields across several objects simultaneously (e.g., a name that might be a Lead, Contact, or Account), which SOQL — tied to one object per query — can't do in a single statement.

questions.q: When would you choose SOSL over SOQL?
options: When you need to update records, since SOQL cannot be used with DML
When you need to search a keyword across multiple unrelated objects at once and aren't sure which object it lives in
When you know the exact object and need precise filtering, sorting, and aggregation
SOSL is always the better choice and should replace SOQL entirely
questions.explain: SOSL is the right tool when you're searching for a piece of text (like a customer's name) and don't know or don't want to specify which single object it belongs to; SOQL is better once you know the object and need structured filtering.

questions.q: What is Data Loader primarily used for?
options: Designing report charts and dashboards
Writing Apex triggers
Bulk inserting, updating, upserting, deleting, or exporting large volumes of records via CSV files, often using the Bulk API
Managing user profiles and permission sets
questions.explain: Data Loader is a client application for high-volume data operations — it maps CSV columns to Salesforce fields and processes records in batches, making it the standard tool for bulk data movement.

questions.q: What makes an upsert operation in Data Loader different from a plain insert or update?
options: Upsert always creates a brand new record and ignores existing ones
Upsert is only available for the Account object
Upsert permanently deletes any record it doesn't recognize
Upsert uses a designated external ID (or the Salesforce Id) to decide whether to update an existing matching record or insert a new one
questions.explain: Upsert checks the specified key field (often a custom External ID field from a source system) against existing records — if a match is found it updates that record, otherwise it inserts a new one, which is ideal for repeatable data loads.

questions.q: Why is it considered best practice to test a bulk delete operation in a sandbox before running it in Data Loader against production?
options: Because deletions move records to the Recycle Bin only temporarily, and a bulk mistake at scale can be costly and slow to fully undo, especially with cascading Master-Detail children
Because Data Loader cannot connect to production orgs at all
Because deletes in Salesforce are always instantly permanent with no Recycle Bin
Because sandboxes automatically prevent all deletions
questions.explain: Deleted records land in the Recycle Bin temporarily, but a large bulk delete — especially one that cascades through Master-Detail children — can be painful to reverse, so validating the operation in a sandbox first is standard practice.

questions.q: What is Workbench primarily used for?
options: Building customer-facing Experience Cloud sites
Running SOQL/SOSL queries, viewing metadata, and performing basic data operations through a browser-based tool, often by admins and developers
Creating Flow automations visually
Managing Stripe billing integrations
questions.explain: Workbench is a free, browser-based utility that lets technical users query data, describe object/field metadata, and run simple data operations without installing a desktop client.

questions.q: What is a key limitation of the Data Import Wizard compared to Data Loader?
options: The Import Wizard can only import from Excel files, never CSV
The Import Wizard requires a paid AppExchange license to use at all
The Import Wizard supports significantly fewer objects and cannot perform deletes, while Data Loader supports nearly any object and full CRUD-style operations
The Import Wizard is only available to System Administrators, unlike Data Loader
questions.explain: The Import Wizard is a simpler, wizard-driven UI limited to a handful of standard/custom objects and insert/update actions with built-in duplicate matching — it can't delete records or handle the breadth of objects Data Loader can.

questions.q: What's the difference between a 15-character and an 18-character Salesforce record Id?
options: The 18-character Id is only used for custom objects
There is no actual difference; both formats are randomly interchangeable
The 15-character Id is used only in sandboxes, the 18-character Id only in production
The 15-character Id is case-sensitive and the 18-character Id adds a case-insensitive checksum suffix so it can be compared safely regardless of letter case
questions.explain: Salesforce Ids are natively 15 characters and case-sensitive; the UI and APIs often surface an 18-character version that appends 3 characters encoding the case of the original 15, making case-insensitive systems compare Ids reliably.

questions.q: What do Salesforce's duplicate and matching rules help an analyst prevent?
options: Users viewing records they don't have permission to see
The creation or import of redundant Lead, Contact, or Account records that represent the same real-world person or company
Reports running slower than expected
Fields exceeding their maximum character length
questions.explain: Matching rules define how Salesforce identifies likely-duplicate records (e.g., by email or company + name), and duplicate rules define what happens when a match is found — alert, block, or allow with a warning.

questions.q: Why does migration sequencing matter — for example, loading Accounts before loading Contacts that reference them?
options: Because Salesforce processes files strictly in alphabetical order regardless of content
Sequencing has no real effect — Salesforce automatically loads records in the correct dependency order
Because a child record's lookup or master-detail field needs a valid parent Id to reference, so the parent must already exist before the child is loaded
Because Account records are always smaller in file size than Contact records
questions.explain: A Contact record referencing an AccountId needs that Account to already exist in the target org; loading children before their parents causes failed rows or orphaned relationship fields, so parents must load first.

questions.q: What is a core part of post-migration validation after loading data into Salesforce?
options: Deleting the source system immediately to avoid confusion
Changing all migrated records' owners to the system administrator
Disabling all validation rules permanently
Comparing record counts and spot-checking key relationships and field values between source and destination to confirm the migration was accurate and complete
questions.explain: Validation means confirming the numbers and the relationships actually match what was migrated — record counts reconciling, lookups pointing at the right parent, and spot-checked values matching the source — before declaring the migration done.

questions.q: A data analyst needs to move 200,000 cleaned Contact records into a new Salesforce org, matching them against an existing External ID to avoid duplicates. Which capability makes this possible in one operation?
options: A SOSL FIND search across the Contact object
A single Workbench SOQL query with no DML
An upsert operation in Data Loader keyed on the External ID field, run at Bulk API scale
A dashboard filter on the Contacts report
questions.explain: This is exactly the upsert pattern data analysts rely on: Data Loader's upsert, keyed to a custom External ID field, updates matching records and inserts new ones in one bulk pass rather than requiring a manual insert/update split.
